    Introduction to presizepo

    presizepo.Rmd
    library(presizepo)

    Overview

    presizepo computes precision-based (confidence-interval width) sample sizes and standard errors for the log odds ratio in a proportional-odds (ordinal logistic regression) model. Two predictor types are supported:

    • a binary group predictor (e.g. treatment vs. control), via se_binary_po() and n_precision_binary_po();
    • a continuous predictor, via se_cont_po() and n_precision_cont_po().

    For both, two calculation methods are available via method:

    • "whitehead" - Whitehead’s (1993) closed-form delta-method variance approximation. Fast, but assumes proportional odds and can be inaccurate for large effects.
    • "ologit" (default) - fits a weighted proportional-odds model directly to the anticipated distribution and reads the standard error off the observed information matrix. This is exact (no delta-method approximation), following White, Marley-Zagar, Morris, Parmar, Royston & Babiker (2023).

    The two methods nearly agree for small effects and diverge as the anticipated effect size grows.

    Binary predictor

    Suppose the anticipated distribution of outcome categories in the control arm is:

    pc <- c(0.15, 0.10, 0.10, 0.10, 0.10, 0.45)

    and we anticipate a proportional odds ratio of 1.7 for the experimental arm relative to control. Instead of OR, the experimental-arm distribution can also be supplied directly via pe, or implied by a common risk ratio rr on the cumulative probabilities; exactly one of OR, pe, rr must be given.

    Standard error at a fixed sample size

    se_binary_po() returns the standard error of the log OR, and a confidence interval for the OR itself, at a given total sample size n (split between arms according to the allocation ratio r):

    se_binary_po(pc, OR = 1.7, n = 200, method = "ologit")
#> $OR
#> [1] 1.7
#> 
#> $conf
#> [1] 0.95
#> 
#> $SE
#> [1] 0.2561491
#> 
#> $lower
#> [1] 1.028998
#> 
#> $upper
#> [1] 2.808558
#> 
#> $method
#> [1] "ologit"
se_binary_po(pc, OR = 1.7, n = 200, method = "whitehead")
#> $OR
#> [1] 1.7
#> 
#> $conf
#> [1] 0.95
#> 
#> $SE
#> [1] 0.2539772
#> 
#> $lower
#> [1] 1.033387
#> 
#> $upper
#> [1] 2.796628
#> 
#> $method
#> [1] "whitehead"

    Sample size for a target precision

    More commonly we want the sample size needed to achieve a target precision, expressed as the ratio of the upper to lower confidence limit for the OR (ratio_UL). n_precision_binary_po() computes this by fitting once at a large reference sample size and rescaling analytically (the Fisher information scales linearly with n):

    n_precision_binary_po(pc, OR = 1.7, ratio_UL = 3, method = "ologit")
#> $n
#> [1] 168
#> 
#> $conf
#> [1] 0.95
#> 
#> $OR
#> [1] 1.7
#> 
#> $method
#> [1] "ologit"
#> 
#> $lci_or
#> [1] 0.9814954
#> 
#> $uci_or
#> [1] 2.944486

    So a sample size of 168 would be needed to constrain the OR’s confidence interval to a 3-fold ratio between its limits.

    Continuous predictor

    For a continuous predictor x, the anticipated outcome-category distribution is instead specified at x = mean(x) (p0), along with the log OR per unit of x (beta) and the SD of x (sd_x):

    p0 <- c(0.10, 0.15, 0.15, 0.20, 0.20, 0.10, 0.10)
se_cont_po(p0, beta = log(1.5), sd_x = 0.5, n = 200, method = "ologit")
#>      beta        SE     lower     upper 
#> 0.4054650 0.2496151 0.9196413 2.4466056

    Here method = "ologit" integrates out the mixing distribution of x (assumed normal) via Gauss-Hermite quadrature (ngrid nodes), jointly estimating the cutpoints and beta; "whitehead" instead evaluates a closed-form variance formula at fixed cutpoints derived from p0.

    An R2 argument allows for the predictor’s effective information to be reduced when other covariates explain some of its variance (e.g. when adjusting for baseline covariates).

    n_precision_cont_po() gives the sample size for a target CI-width ratio, expressed for the OR per delta units of x:

    n_precision_cont_po(p0, beta = log(1.5), sd_x = 0.5, ratio_UL = 3,
                     delta = 1, method = "ologit")
#> $n
#> [1] 159
#> 
#> $or
#> [1] 1.5
#> 
#> $method
#> [1] "ologit"
#> 
#> $lci
#> [1] 0.8660254
#> 
#> $uci
#> [1] 2.598076

    Choosing a method

    "ologit" is the exact calculation and is the default; "whitehead" is faster and closed-form but relies on a delta-method approximation that can understate uncertainty for larger anticipated effects. When in doubt, compare both, as done above, and prefer "ologit" if they diverge meaningfully.

    References

    Whitehead, J. (1993). Sample size calculations for ordered categorical data. Statistics in Medicine, 12(24), 2257-2271.

    White, I. R., Marley-Zagar, E., Morris, T. P., Parmar, M. K., Royston, P., & Babiker, A. (2023). A simple software-based approach to sample size calculation for ordinal outcomes. Statistical Methods in Medical Research. doi:10.1177/1536867X231162228
